name: C10-5
question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.

turns.text: I think Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units. Reasons I expect to hold up: (1) tenants in these units are poor and have no bargaining power, so landlords can raise rents freely; (2) the living conditions are unsafe and crowded, and affordable alternatives are scarce; (3) a rent cap can be paired with safety rules so that it protects people rather than just cutting supply.

You said tenants have no bargaining power, so landlords can raise rents freely — but you also said a rent cap can be paired with safety rules without cutting supply. What connects the cap to the safety rules in your reasoning?

My idea is that if landlords have to meet safety rules, they also need some money back, so the cap should be set high enough to allow that, but still stop sudden big rises. I am not sure it works though. Can you show me sources from the archive?

You've said the cap should be high enough to let landlords cover safety costs but still block sudden big rises — which of those two halves feels shakier to you right now?

And for that shakier half, what would a source need to show you: evidence that costs really are that high, a counter-view that caps don't stop rises, or a case where a cap played out?
The shakier half is that a cap stops big rises. I would like a source about a case where a cap played out in Hong Kong, and also a counter-view that caps make landlords leave or cut supply.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling supply elasticity, distinguishing first- and second-generation controls, with Hong Kong-like simulations.
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Comparative case study of Berlin's 2020-2021 rent cap, describing supply effects and legal outcome.
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Data excerpt from an index tracking SDU stock and rents from 2019 to 2025, with caveats.
- D5: Submission: Landlords Association of Hong Kong (Stakeholder submission). Stakeholder submission from a landlords' association arguing against hard caps, with self-reported data.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report based on a tenant survey, arguing for tenure security over hard caps.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
D6 is a model of whether caps cut supply with Hong Kong-like cases, D2 is actual rent data so I can check if rises happened, and D5 is the landlords' counter-view I asked for.

I read D6, D2 and D5. My position is refined: the existing Hong Kong rule only limits rises inside a tenancy (D6p2) and stock kept growing (D2p1), so a moderate tightening looks safe, but a hard cap on starting rent looks risky (D6p1, D5p2). Rents still rose faster than general rents (D2p2) and burden got worse, so the current rule is not enough. The landlords' evidence is weak though (D5p3). What is the strongest opposing view to my position?

Document D6, the working paper on rent control and supply elasticity, argues that the stable stock you cite from D2 is an artifact of a non-binding instrument, and that a binding cap behaves differently — contraction falls on the same households the cap aims to protect.

How do you answer this?

I agree a binding hard cap would hurt the people it is meant to help (D6p3), so I would not do that. My answer is to tighten the second-generation type: lower the allowed rise inside tenancies and make the rule cover small tenancies too, since D2p3 says reporting is voluntary below the threshold. That keeps the protection without forcing exits. But I still need to know if tenants actually gain, so I want another view, maybe the NGO or Berlin.

You've said what you want the source to do — show whether tenants actually gain — and you've named the claim it's for: that tightening the second-generation rule keeps protection without forcing exits.

What would count as "tenants actually gain" in your essay: lower rents, fewer evictions, longer tenancies, or something else?
Mostly longer tenancies and fewer forced moves, because a poor tenant mainly fears being pushed out, plus rents that stay affordable relative to income. Please show me sources on that.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Offers material on this topic.
- D8: Comparative Note: New York City Rent Stabilisation (Comparative case). Comparative case note on New York's second-generation rent stabilisation scheme and its long-run effects.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modelling supply elasticity and welfare under first- versus second-generation rent controls.
- D3: Tenant Interview: Mr Chan, Kwai Chung (Interview). Interview transcript giving a tenant's lived experience of insecurity and views on rent caps.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report surveying tenant preferences and arguing for tenure security over hard caps.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
D8 is about a second-generation scheme over the long run, which is the type I favour; D3 is a real tenant's view on insecurity; D11 surveys tenants on tenure security, which is my measure of gain.

Unlocked: D8 (Comparative Note: New York City Rent Stabilisation), D3 (Tenant Interview: Mr Chan, Kwai Chung), D11 (NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First). You can now read their passages by id, for example D8p1.

These change my position. I still say tighten, but the tightening should be about security of tenure (D3p1, D11p1) and the tenancy rise limit (D8p2), not rent levels. Tenants themselves care more about the queue and not being thrown out (D3p3, D11p1) than about cheaper rent. New York shows a cost too: less upkeep and fewer listings after tightening (D8p3). So I keep the direction but change the target. Can you give me structure options for the essay?

Three tracks:

1. Claim, evidence, objection, reply — good when your main move is defending a refined position against the strongest counter.
2. Problem, cause, response — good when you want the reader to feel why the current rule fails before you propose the fix.
3. Compare and contrast — good when the New York and Berlin cases carry the argument and Hong Kong is the test.

Which one fits what you want to say, and why?
I pick option 1, claim, evidence, objection, reply, because my position is a refined one and the main task is to defend it against the supply-loss objection from D6 and the landlords.

Good — that track fits a refined position. Now decide what the objection section has to carry: is it only D6's supply-loss point, or also the New York upkeep and listing cost from D8p3?

And where does the landlords' weak evidence (D5p3) sit — inside your evidence, or inside your reply?

The objection carries both: D6 supply loss and the D8 upkeep and listing cost. The landlords' weak evidence goes in the reply, as a reason not to take their exit threat at full face value, though I still accept the risk is real. I think I have enough turns of thinking; one more check: is there anything in the archive on enforcement or inspection that I should use?

You've said the landlords' evidence is weak and that you'll use it in the reply — what would a source on enforcement or inspection need to show for that reply: that the threat is overstated, or that it's real but manageable?
It would need to show the threat is real but manageable, for example that inspection and tenure rules can be enforced cheaply. Please list what the archive has.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Data excerpt tracking SDU stock and rents over time, with caveats on post-2023 survey extrapolation.
- D10: Internal Minute: Housing Authority Enforcement Subcommittee (draft, not for circulation) (Internal minute). Internal enforcement subcommittee minute, draft and not for circulation, focused on inspection capacity and register feasibility.
- D9: Legal Opinion: Compensation and Judicial Review Risk (Legal opinion). Legal opinion from counsel on compensation and judicial review risks of rent caps.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report based on tenant survey, arguing for tenure security over hard rent caps.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper reviewing supply elasticity literature and modeling tightened cap scenarios.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.

D9 is a legal opinion on compensation risk, which tests whether my tightening is legally manageable. I am skipping D10 because it is marked draft and not for circulation, so I should not rely on it in an essay.
Unlocked: D9 (Legal Opinion: Compensation and Judicial Review Risk). You can now read their passages by id, for example D9p1.
D9p1

D9 supports my refined view: a hard cap on starting rent risks compensation claims (D9p1), while rules on tenancy terms are on firmer ground. A light band could be a later step but needs survey data that does not exist yet (D9p2). So I will recommend tenure security and a tighter rise limit first, and a band only after data is built.

You've said D9 supports the refined view and that the band waits on data. What would you want D9p1 and D9p2 to show for your reply section — that the compensation risk is confined to starting-rent caps, or that it also touches the rise limit?

drafts.text:
I think Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units, but not by capping rent levels. The tightening should protect tenants from being pushed out and limit rises inside a tenancy.

A hard cap is risky. A working paper finds that supply of this kind of housing falls when controlled rents fall, by about 3 to 5 percent of stock for a 10 percent cut [D6p1]. The people who lose units are the same people the cap is meant to help [D6p3]. Landlords say they would leave the market [D5p2], although their data is weak and self-reported [D5p3].

The current rule only limits rises inside a tenancy, and stock kept growing after it [D2p1, D6p2]. But rents still rose faster than general rents and rent burden got worse [D2p2]. So the current rule is not enough.

Tenants care about security. Mr Chan says insecurity is worse than price [D3p1], and a survey found 61 percent would accept a rent increase for three years of security [D11p1].

Position: tighten, but target tenure security and rises within tenancies, not a hard cap on starting rent.

Evidence: current rule limits rises in tenancies, stock kept growing [D2p1, D6p2], but rents rose faster than general rents and burden worsened [D2p2]. Tenants want security [D3p1, D11p1] and the queue [D3p3].

Objection: hard caps cut supply [D6p1, D6p3], legal risk [D9p1], New York upkeep and listings cost [D8p3].

Reply: landlord exit threat is weakly evidenced [D5p3] but real [D5p2]; second-generation rules have small effects on stock [D8p2]; use band later only after data [D9p2].
